Kamuli District in Eastern Uganda has a population of about 500,000 people, with a large proportion being children i.e. about 130,000 are primary school-going age (6–12 years) and 90% of these are enrolled in primary schools. Applying national disability prevalence rates, around 13% i.e. 15,000 primary school children are living with disabilities. These children face challenges such as limited access to inclusive classrooms, inadequate appropriate learning materials, and social stigma, which often hinder their full participation in education despite the district’s high enrolment under Universal Primary Education. Thid is further exacerbated by limited Play Based Learning (PBL) Between 2020–2023, Cordaid, in collaboration with Uganda’s Ministry of Education and Sports, implemented a Performance-Based Financing (PBF) project in 50 primary schools in Kamuli District. Schools were financially rewarded on 33 aspects to stimulate equitable access, quality of education, and governance, ultimately to improve child education outcomes. Enrolment rose by 21%—from 25,019 to 30,216—driven by an improved learning environment, giving higher incentives for enrolling girls and children with disabilities. By 2023, 47 schools had plans to re-enrol dropouts, all schools had at least five new teaching aids per classroom and new educational signage on school compounds, and desk availability improved significantly. A major lesson from the previous PBF project was the urgent need for strengthening Play Based Learning (PBL) and disability inclusion in primary schools. Despite growing recognition of its benefits, the implementation of PBL in Uganda is hindered by several systemic and contextual barriers. Many schools, particularly in rural areas, lack basic infrastructure and materials such as toys, books, and safe play spaces, making it difficult to integrate play into the curriculum. Additionally, cultural attitudes often undervalue play as a legitimate educational tool, with some parents and educators viewing it as a distraction from "serious" learning. Teachers themselves frequently lack the training and support needed to effectively facilitate play-based approaches. primary schools in Busoga region- Kamuli district are majorly characterized of high teacher- learner ratio, inadequate/ lack or teaching aids and learning materials that promote Play (PBL).
Moreso, both physical and social barriers continue to limit girls and Children With Disabilities (CWD) from a conducive learning environment. About 13% of children in Uganda live with a disability (UBOS, 2014 Census) and are among the most marginalized; less likely to attend school, access health care, or be protected from abuse (UNICEF, 2022). In Kamuli District, the most common types of disabilities among school-age children include visual impairments, hearing difficulties, physical disabilities, learning or intellectual disabilities and albinism among others. Whereas some of the children with severe disabilities will need to be referred to specialised schools of children with disabilities, majority have mild to moderate disabilities and require proper integration in existing primary school. As a result of the earlier stated barriers that are both physical and social in nature, there are children with disabilities in Kamuli who do not attend school at all. Some remain at home due to mobility challenges, lack of supportive infrastructure and family perceptions that education is not accessible or useful for them. This exclusion contributes to lower literacy and educational attainment among children with disabilities compared to their peers. This further justifies the urgent need for disability inclusion both at school and community level.
